cells.tense: You are holding this steady right now, and it is not costing you a thing.
cells.act: let yourself be reached by what they are carrying
cells.ask: When someone close to you is sitting in something heavy, let it reach you before you do anything about it — stay in contact a while, no fixing, no lifting.
cells.core:
You can tell what needs your weight and what doesn't, and you do it without straining. A friend comes to you in trouble and you hold it steady; you don't go hard, you don't lecture, you don't turn their mess into your worry. That's what bearing something well looks like — the shape stays, nothing snaps, nothing turns to stone.

What this balance is free to feed next is being reached. Most people holding a hard thing are already bracing before it lands; you have the calm to let it land. So when someone close to you is sitting in something heavy, let it reach you before you do anything about it. Stay in contact a while, and don't fix or lift it. There's a version of held where you stay soft, and this is the week to find it.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold what's heavy and stay human while you do it.
cells.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
cells.place: the place where weight and attention land before any reasoning has arrived

cells.tense: You will have braced for something that hasn't happened yet, and the bracing is the hurt.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Find a place where you're holding tighter than the situation asks. Put it in fair proportion — enough and no more — and when it's right, quit.
cells.core:
The grip is running ahead of you. Somewhere past the next bend a thing might go wrong, and your body already has its hands around it — holding the friend upright before they've stumbled, holding the plan before the week has spoken, holding a door shut on something that may not come. What used to be strength is setting like concrete. The tighter you hold, the less you hear what's actually there, and the people you're holding upright can feel the squeeze.

Restoring proportion is the work. Locate one place where you're holding tighter than the situation asks. Put it in fair proportion — enough and no more — then quit while it's right. You've been hauling weight for ground nobody has stood on yet, and setting it down is how the hands remember they're hands.
cells.sheetLine: You're gripping next week before it has arrived.
cells.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
cells.place: the place where weight and attention land before any reasoning has arrived

cells.tense: You were holding so much pressure for so long that putting anything down felt like it would finally finish you.
cells.act: release it on purpose, not by losing it
cells.ask: Take something you've kept a grip on and set it down deliberately — not a slip, a choice — then leave your hands open a day or two.
cells.core:
When the pressure came, holding wasn't safe anymore — you couldn't take the extra weight and you didn't let anyone see that, so what happened is you stopped taking weight at all. Something goes wrong now and the hands don't reach. You stand near the door, past the moment, telling yourself there's nothing you can add. The strength hasn't gone; the grip went, and behind the not-reaching there's a decision already made that whatever you hold will get crushed or taken.

Release skipped its proper place — it moved in before the job was finished. Take something you've kept a grip on. Set it down deliberately, not by losing it, and leave your hands empty for a day or two. Ending a hold on purpose is not the same as having nothing to hold, and the body learns the difference only by doing it.
cells.sheetLine: You stopped reaching, not because you can't hold, but because holding stopped feeling safe.
cells.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
cells.place: the place where weight and attention land before any reasoning has arrived

cells.tense: You are already the steady presence in the room, and when someone says so you credit the situation rather than the hands.
cells.act: remember what drew you and face it again
cells.ask: Think of something you used to move toward before the steadying began — a craft, a place, a person — and face it again plainly, for its own sake.
cells.core:
There's holding happening in your life that you'd put on the situation rather than on yourself. Someone falls apart and you keep your feet; you'd say anyone would. The room holds because you keep holding it, and that you can is not something you claim. What's harder to see is the second thing riding along: the aim. Strength needs somewhere to point, and yours is still pointed where it was before you learned to brace — which is why nothing arranged feels finished.

The part of you that knew where to face came before you got good at carrying. Think of something you used to move toward before the steadying took over — a craft, a town, a person, a stretch of work you actually wanted. Face it again plainly, not as a duty. That pull is yours; it was there before the shoulders were.
cells.sheetLine: You steady the room and call it nothing. The aiming is also you.
cells.verb: bearing what has to be borne without hardening around it
cells.place: the place where weight and attention land before any reasoning has arrived

attempts.check: The draft says this person can tell what deserves the holding and what doesn't in real time — the seat is the capacity to attend, not a track record, so the record doesn't support a claim about their judgment being good, only about where the holding landed. A reader could reasonably object that steadying a friend is just being kind, and that the body-holding part is being smuggled in. The ask survives being wrong: sitting with someone in it without fixing anything teaches the person where they reach for grabbing, whether or not my read of the seat holds. The sentence that serves me more than the person is any line that makes steady holding sound like wisdom itself — wiser than the room — and I've kept it out.
